pr.title: Plan a sidebar list of a plan's sections and its nearby projects
pr.head: ff11e3d64f79763372b07446453d740815e6e0bc

summary: Projector's site gives each project a page that renders its plan, the readme.md under docs/projects/<name>/. The project-page-nav plan, in #219 beneath this pull request, gives that page the sidebar a pull request summary already has: the project as a header, its stacks of pull requests, the project's other pages, and a footer row.

That plan leaves two things out on purpose, and this pull request records a plan for them. First, a summary's sidebar lists its numbered sections so a reader can jump to any of them, but a project page's sidebar would list none, though the longest plans here run 500 to 800 lines. Second, a nested project's sidebar lists only its own pages, so reaching a sibling project means going back through the breadcrumbs.

The new plan, project-page-sections, is a draft at priority later. It settles nothing. For each question it lays out the options and their trade-offs, and its § 3 lists six questions for the user. The plan moves to ready once they are answered. The pull request changes no code.

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• Sidebar: the boxed column at the left of a summary page, and, under project-page-nav, of a project page. sideNavHtml is the shared helper that plan adds to draw it.
  • Section list: the summary sidebar's <ol> of links to its sections, each row a number (nnum), a title (ntitle), and a reviewed dot (ncheck).
  • slug: the function in site/src/site.ts that turns a rendered heading's text into its id, the anchor a link like #2-solution lands on.
  • Nested project: a project inside another project's folder, with its own readme.md.

cards.title: The six open questions
cards.html:
1. Where the headings come from: read from the rendered plan, extracted at build time, or both (§ 2.1).
  2. How the sidebar's links match the ids the rendered headings get (§ 2.2).
  3. Which heading levels to list, and how to show a plan's own section numbers (§ 2.3).
  4. Whether to mark the section you are scrolled to, and on summary pages too (§ 2.4).
  5. What a nested project's sidebar lists (§ 2.6).
  6. How the sections and the pages share the sidebar, and whether a supplemental page lists its own sections (§ 2.7, § 2.8).

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html: The Projector review of this head is clean, with no finding threads. A draft plan makes no readiness claim, so its open questions do not block. The review left three suggestions, shown as notes under the lines they concern.

groups.title: The project-page-sections plan
groups.kicker: A draft plan that lays out the options for a sidebar section list and sibling navigation
intro: The plan has the shape every Projector plan has: § 1 states the problem, § 2 the solution, then open questions and background. Here § 2 is a survey rather than a design. Each subsection asks one question, usually with a table of options and trade-offs.

• § 2.1 and § 2.2, data. The browser has a plan's headings only after it renders the Markdown, so the list either waits for the render or comes from the build, which then has to produce the same ids the browser's slug gives the rendered headings.
  • § 2.3 to § 2.5, the list itself. Which levels to show, whether to mark the current section with an IntersectionObserver, and a shared sectionListHtml beside sideNavHtml so the summary and the plan draw one list.
  • § 2.6 to § 2.8, layout. What a nested project's sidebar lists, how the section list and the project's pages share the sidebar, and pages that have no sections.

checks.text: Read this beside docs/projects/project-page-nav/readme.md from #219. That plan's opening paragraph and its § 3, "Why this design", name project-page-sections as where the section list and sibling navigation are settled, and this plan's § 1 restates both gaps as that plan describes them.

files.note: The whole plan: a draft that surveys the options for listing a plan's sections and its nearby projects in a project page's sidebar.

checks.text: project check prints Project plans are valid., and project list shows the plan as draft under later. Both were run at this head.

§ 2.1, first option. showDocument already redraws the whole frame, sidebar included, when the Markdown arrives, replacing the Loading… page. A list read from the rendered plan would appear in that same redraw, so only the sidebar blocks below it move, at the moment the plan itself appears. The review suggested saying so, since it makes this option's cost smaller than the row states.

§ 2.2 describes slug as it is at this head: text.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/[^\w\s-]/g, '').replace(/\s+/g, '-'), applied by renderMarkdown to every heading without an id, with no step that tells two identical headings apart.
§ 2.4 is right that a summary page marks no current section: the only IntersectionObserver in site/src/summary.ts pins section and file headers as they stick.

§ 2.7, Length. This weighs only the wide layout. At 980 pixels and narrower, summary.css makes the sidebar static and project-page-nav puts it before the plan, so a long section list pushes the plan down the page. The review suggested adding that case, since it bears on question 6.

§ 4. The counts were taken on the stack's base. main has since gained proposed-projects, with 6 ### subsections, so eight plans there hold subsections rather than seven. The range of 4 to 14 ## sections and the maximum of 8 subsections still hold.
